units.title: The Circulatory System
units.intro:
Double circulation: heart → lungs → heart (pulmonary) and heart → body → heart (systemic). Right side is deoxygenated; left is oxygenated. Valves stop back-flow.

Path: body veins → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

lessons.title: The Human Heart and Types of Circulation

cards.title: More detail — heart beat and blood
body: Walls: left ventricle is thickest because it pushes systemic pressure. Atria are thinner receiving rooms. AV valves (tricuspid right, bicuspid/mitral left) stop ventricle-to-atrium backflow. Semilunar valves stop artery-to-ventricle backflow. “Lub-dup” is valves closing.

Heartbeat: atria fill, atria squeeze, ventricles squeeze, pause. Coronary arteries feed the heart muscle itself — a clot there is a heart attack. Pulse is an artery expanding with each ventricle beat.

Red cells: no nucleus in mature human RBCs, packed with haemoglobin. White cells: some phagocytose, some make antibodies. Platelets are fragments. Plasma is pale yellow. Anaemia = too little haemoglobin or too few RBCs. Clotting needs platelets + plasma factors + calcium; hemophilia is a factor missing.

cards.title: 2.1.1 The Human Heart
body: The heart functions as a pump and is responsible for the circulation of blood through the blood vessels.
The heart produces the pressure responsible for making blood flow through the blood vessels by contracting forcefully.
The right side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs, where carbon dioxide is exchanged for oxygen.
Carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the lungs and oxygen diffuses from the lungs into the blood.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Types of Circulation
body: In general, in animals there are two types of circulations: open and closed circulation.
The open type of circulation is found in insects, in which the blood does not flow through blood vessels.
In an open circulatory system, blood pumped by the heart is emptied into large blood-filled spaces.
As the body cells are bathed in blood, materials diffuse out of the blood and into each cell through the cell membrane.

cards.title: 2.1.3 Blood Circuits
body: The pulmonary artery, arising from the right ventricle, divides into two branches, one leading to the right lung and the other to the left.
The oxygenated blood from the lungs enters the left atrium through the four pulmonary veins.
A contraction of the left ventricle pushes blood against the bicuspid valve, closing it, and against the aortic semilunar valve, opening it and allowing blood to enter the aorta.
The blood from all parts of the body returns to the right atrium by way of two large veins.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following blood vessels carries deoxygenated blood from the upper regions of the body (head and neck) directly back to the right atrium?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the roles of systemic veins returning to the heart**
The blood from all parts of the body returns to the right atrium by way of two large veins. These are the superior vena cava, which drains blood from regions of the head and neck; and the inferior vena cava, which drains blood from the lower regions of the body."

**Final Result:**
**Superior vena cava**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following structures is absent in healthy human arteries but present in systemic veins to prevent the backward flow of blood under low pressure?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Compare structures of arteries and veins**
* Both arteries and veins have three tissue layers (endothelium, smooth muscle, and elastic/connective tissue).
* Arteries carry blood under high pressure and do not have internal valves.
* Many veins, particularly those in the upper and lower limbs, contain valves all along their length... These valves aid in returning blood to the heart because they open as long as the flow is toward the heart, but close if it is in the opposite direction."

**Final Result:**
**One-way valves**.

cards.title: ARTERY = Away
body: Arteries leave the heart. Veins visit the heart. Pulmonary names are the exceptions for oxygen, not for direction.

cards.title: 2.2.1 Arteries
body: The arteries and arterioles conduct blood away from the ventricles of the heart and lead to the capillaries.
The wall of arteries consists of three distinct layers.
The innermost layer is composed of a layer of simple epithelium, called endothelium.
The middle layer makes up the bulk of the arterial wall.

cards.title: 2.2.2 Veins
body: The vessels of the venous system begin with the merging of capillaries into venules.
Venules then combine into small veins and small veins into larger ones.
Venules are the microscopic vessels that branch out from the capillaries and merge to form veins.
Around the body organs, blood passes into venules.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Capillaries
body: The pressure of the blood in the capillaries forces fluid out of the capillaries.
Oxygen, glucose and other nutrients diffuse from the blood into the tissue fluid and then into the cells.
Waste products, such as urea and carbon dioxide, diffuse from the cells into the tissue fluid, and then into the blood.
Tissue fluid can also pass into the blood by osmosis, carrying with it dissolved waste products.

options.A: To chemically digest leaked plasma proteins.
options.B: To prevent the backflow of blood from ventricles to atria.
options.C: To reduce friction between the pericardium and the contracting heart.
options.D: To oxygenate the cardiac muscle cells of the left ventricle.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Refer to the definition of pericardium and its fluid**
The pericardial fluid present between the pericardium and the heart itself reduces friction between them."

**Step 2: Contrast with incorrect options**
* Digesting proteins is not a function of pericardial fluid.

**Final Result:**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following valves prevents the backflow of blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium during ventricular contraction (systole)?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Locate the valves in each heart chamber**
* The **tricuspid valve** is located between the right atrium and the right ventricle.
* The **bicuspid (mitral) valve** is located between the left atrium and the left ventricle.
* The **semilunar valves** prevent backflow from the great arteries (aorta and pulmonary artery) into the ventricles.

**Step 2: Identify the valve that matches the question's criteria**
During left ventricular contraction, blood attempts to flow back into the left atrium; the bicuspid (mitral) valve closes to prevent this backflow.

**Final Result:**
**Bicuspid (mitral) valve**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Understand valve function. Bicuspid (mitral) and tricuspid valves are Atrioventricular (AV) valves.
**Step 2:** They prevent backflow from ventricles to atria.
**Step 3:** Therefore, they must close when the ventricles contract (**ventricular systole**) to ensure blood goes into the arteries (Aorta/Pulmonary) instead of back to the atria.

steps.text: **Step 1.** **Step 1:** List the valves in the human heart.

**Step 2.** There are four main valves: the **Tricuspid** valve, the **Pulmonary** valve, the **Mitral** (bicuspid) valve, and the **Aortic** valve.
**Step 2:** Match the count with the options.
**Step 3.** The total is 4.

cards.title: Blood Composition
body: **Blood:** plasma (water, salts, proteins, CO₂, hormones, glucose) + red cells (haemoglobin, O₂) + white cells (defence) + platelets (clotting).

cards.title: 2.3.1 Plasma
body: Plasma is the clear, straw-coloured, liquid portion of the blood in which the cells and platelets are suspended.
Blood plasma constitutes about 55% of the total volume of blood.
By maintaining this balance, plasma is an important agent of homeostasis.
Plasma proteins are the most abundant dissolved substances (solutes) in plasma.

cards.title: 2.3.2 Blood Cells
body: Blood cells, which are formed mostly in the bone marrow, include red blood cells (erythrocytes), white blood cells (leukocytes) and cellular fragments called blood platelets (thrombocytes).
Red Blood Cells (Red Corpuscles) Red blood cells are tiny, biconcave discs that are thin near the centres and thicker around the rim.
Because of its shape, a red blood cell can also deform readily as it squeezes through the narrow passages of capillaries.
When haemoglobin combines with oxygen, the resulting oxyhaemoglobin is bright red, and when the oxygen is released, the resulting deoxyhaemoglobin is darker.

options.B: To produce specific globulin antibodies to destroy bacteria.
options.C: To maintain the constant pH and water potential of plasma.

Platelets play an important role in preventing blood loss (or in blood clotting). This prevention is accomplished in two ways: 1. The formation of platelet plugs... 2. The formation of clots..."

cards.why: **Thrombocytes** is the scientific name for **platelets**. They are cell fragments involved in blood clotting (hemostasis) to prevent excessive bleeding after an injury.

cards.title: 2.4 Blood Clotting
body: When there is an injury to the blood vessels, several actions help prevent excessive blood loss.
Injury to a larger vessel may result in a severe haemorrhage that requires special treatment.
When an arteriole or a venule is cut or broken, the smooth muscles in the wall are stimulated to contract and blood loss lessens almost immediately.
Platelets stick to exposed ends of injured blood vessels.
When platelets come into contact with collagen, their shapes change drastically and numerous spiny processes begin to protrude from their membranes.

cards.title: Blood Clotting
body: Clotting: damage → platelets plug → cascade → fibrin mesh traps cells. Blood groups (A B AB O, plus Rh) matter because antibodies in plasma attack the wrong antigen — match before transfusion.

cards.q: Which of the following blood types is known as the 'universal recipient' because its plasma lacks both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, allowing it to receive blood from any ABO type safely?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Check blood type characteristics**
* Because type AB blood lacks both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, a type AB person can receive a blood transfusion from any other type. For this reason, type AB persons are called universal recipients."

**Final Result:**
**Type AB**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the name of the inherited blood disorder characterized by a lack of clotting factors (specifically thromboplastin), leading to a dangerously delayed clotting time?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define the disorders listed**
* Atherosclerosis: fat deposits in vessel walls.
* Haemophilia: Haemophilia: This is a condition resulting from a lack of adequate quantities of thromboplastin... the clotting time of the blood may delay to the point where a loss of blood becomes dangerous. Haemophilia is an inheritable condition."
* Erythroblastosis: hemolytic destruction of fetal RBCs.
* Anaemia: deficiency of RBCs or hemoglobin.

**Final Result:**
**Haemophilia**.

cards.q: Which of the following blood type(s) could safely be given to someone with O$$^+$$ blood?
cards.why: A person with **O$$^+$$** blood can receive blood from **O$$^+$$** (identical type) and **O$$^-$$** (the universal donor). They cannot receive A, B, or AB because they have anti-A and anti-B antibodies.

cards.title: 2.5 Blood Types
body: Conditions like haemorrhage, wound, shock, severe burns and various illnesses may require a blood transfusion.
If whole blood is used, the patient receives both the necessary plasma and blood cells.
A transfusion of human blood was for the first time attempted in the 1800s.
By the late 1800s, an Austrian physician, Karl Landsteiner, began investigating the reason for this.
In 1900, he determined that there are different types of blood and that only certain combinations of them are compatible.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which specific circulatory circuit is responsible for delivering deoxygenated blood to the lung alveoli to release carbon dioxide and absorb oxygen?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define the function of each circuit**
* Systemic circulation supplies blood to the body organs.
* Coronary circulation supplies the heart muscle.
* Pulmonary circulation specifically goes from the heart to the lungs and back.

**Final Result:**
**Pulmonary circulation**.

cards.q: What is the condition called when a stationary blood clot (thrombus) breaks away from a vessel wall and floats freely through the bloodstream, potentially causing a stroke if it blocks a brain artery?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Differentiate thrombus and embolus**
Such a clot is called a thrombus... If a thrombus breaks away from a blood vessel and travels around the body, it becomes a floating clot, called an embolus. This clot may eventually lodge in another organ. For example a paralytic stroke may be caused by a small embolus..."

**Final Result:**
**Embolus**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: _____________is a type of circulation, which **purifies** the blood.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand circulation types.** 
- **Systemic circulation:** Carries oxygenated blood to the body and returns deoxygenated blood to the heart.
- **Pulmonary circulation:** Carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs to pick up oxygen and release carbon dioxide (purification).
**Step 2: Conclusion.** Pulmonary circulation is the process that purifies the blood in the lungs.

tips.text: The human circulatory system involves the transportation of nutrients, oxygen, hormones, vitamins and other useful substances to all cells of the body.
The circulatory system also facilitates the removal of waste substances that result from the metabolic reactions of each cell of the body.
The system has a pumping organ, to force the flow of materials to each and every cell of the body.
All the materials that need to be transported to or from the cells are mixed in a blood medium.
Blood flows through the blood vessels and because of this human blood circulation is referred to as a closed type of circulation.
In the case of insects, as blood does not flow through blood vessels, the type of circulation is open.
The two upper chambers, called atria, have relatively thin walls.
The two lower chambers, called ventricles, have much thicker, muscular walls.
The wall of the left ventricle is thicker than the wall of the right.
Blood from the right ventricle is pumped to the lungs through the pulmonary artery and returns to the left atrium via the pulmonary veins.

questions.q: Which ventricle is thicker and why?
questions.answer: Left — it drives the long high-pressure systemic circuit.
why: The left ventricle pumps blood all around the body (systemic circulation) at high pressure, so it has a much thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle, which pumps only to the nearby lungs.

similar.q: The systemic circuit extends  A) from the heart to the lungs.  B) from the heart to the coronary arteries only.  C) from the heart to the body's organs and tissues.  D) from the gastrointestinal tract to the liver.  E) from the heart to the kidneys.
similar.a: C. from the heart to the body's organs and tissues. — B, D and E are only parts of the systemic circuit (coronary, hepatic portal and renal circulations).

questions.q: Pulmonary artery is special because?
questions.answer: It leaves the heart but carries deoxygenated blood.
why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; usually it is oxygenated, but the pulmonary artery takes deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
questions.label: 2. Pulmonary artery is special because?

similar.q: Blood returning to the heart from the body organs enters into the  A) left atrium through the aorta.  B) right atrium through the vena cava.  C) left ventricle by the pulmonary artery.  D) right ventricle by the pulmonary vein.  E) right atrium by pulmonary vein.
similar.a: B. right atrium through the vena cava. — The aorta carries blood away from the left ventricle; pulmonary veins bring blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Answer: B.

questions.q: Pulmonary vein is special because?
questions.answer: It enters the heart carrying oxygenated blood.
why: Veins carry blood to the heart; usually it is deoxygenated, but the pulmonary vein brings oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
questions.label: 3. Pulmonary vein is special because?

similar.q: The arteries supplying blood to the tissues of the heart are the  A) renal arteries.  B) coronary arteries.  C) pulmonary arteries.  D) vena cavae.  E) hepatic arteries.
similar.a: B. coronary arteries. — Renal → kidneys; hepatic → liver; pulmonary arteries carry blood to the lungs; venae cavae are veins. Answer: B.

questions.q: Valve between left atrium and ventricle?
why: The left atrioventricular valve has two flaps (cusps), so it is called the bicuspid (mitral) valve; the right one has three (tricuspid).

questions.q: What do semilunar valves prevent?
questions.answer: Blood falling back from aorta / pulmonary artery into ventricles.
why: Semilunar valves at the bases of the aorta and pulmonary artery close when the ventricles relax, stopping blood flowing back into the ventricles.

questions.q: Name the three vessel types.
why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, and capillaries are the tiny vessels between them where exchange with the tissues takes place.

why: Capillary walls are only one cell thick, so oxygen, glucose and wastes have a very short distance to diffuse between blood and tissue cells.

questions.q: A Grade 10 student in Asmara observes a prepared slide of body tissue and sees very narrow vessels whose walls are only one cell thick. Which structural feature of these vessels allows them to carry out the exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes between the blood and the tissue fluid?

options.A: They are made of a single layer of simple endothelium, one cell thick
options.B: They are made of three thick, muscular and elastic layers that resist high pressure
options.C: They contain one-way valves along their whole length to prevent backflow
options.D: They have a wide lumen that carries blood away from the heart at high speed

why: **Identify the vessel described.** The vessels described are microscopic and their walls are one cell thick, which is the defining structure of capillaries: microscopic vessels made of a single layer of simple endothelium.

**Recall the function of capillaries.** Capillaries are the only vessels whose thin, semi-permeable walls allow nutrients, respiratory gases and wastes to diffuse between the blood and the surrounding tissue fluid.

**Test each distractor.** Three thick muscular elastic layers describes arteries, not capillaries. One-way valves along the length describe veins, not capillaries. A wide lumen carrying blood away from the heart at high speed again describes an artery, and capillaries do not carry blood away from the heart.
**Conclude.** Only option A correctly states the one-cell-thick simple endothelium, which provides the short diffusion path required for exchange between blood and tissues.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: Blood leaving the left ventricle is forced into the aorta at high pressure. Which structural feature of arteries is an adaptation to this high pressure?
questions.answer: A. Walls made of thick, muscular and highly elastic tissue in three layers
why: **Recall the function of arteries.** Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure, so their walls must be able to stretch and recoil without bursting.

**Match structure to function.** Arteries have thick, muscular and highly elastic walls composed of three layers, an adaptation that withstands and smooths the high-pressure surge of each ventricular contraction.

**Eliminate wrong options.** A single layer of simple endothelium describes capillaries; valves at intervals describe veins; a narrow lumen that slows blood before it reaches the tissues contradicts the need for rapid one-way delivery.
**Conclude.** The correct choice is A, the three-layered thick, elastic muscular wall.

questions.q: Deoxygenated blood leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary artery on its way to the lungs. Which statement best explains why the pulmonary artery is an exception to the usual rule about arteries?
questions.answer: A. It carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart
why: **State the general rule.** Arteries always carry blood away from the heart and veins always carry blood back towards the heart.

**Apply the rule to the pulmonary artery.** The pulmonary artery arises from the right ventricle and carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs, so it follows the direction rule but breaks the common assumption that arterial blood is oxygenated.
**Check the returning vessel.** Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs to the left atrium through the pulmonary veins, which are veins carrying oxygenated blood.
**Conclude.** Option A is correct: the vessel carries blood away from the heart, but that blood is deoxygenated.

questions.q:
A student in Keren cuts his hand while chopping firewood. The wound bleeds and then stops after a short time. Complete the statements below about the third stage of hemostasis (coagulation) by writing the missing terms.
Injured tissues and platelets release (i) ______. In the presence of calcium ions ($$Ca^{2+}$$) and Vitamin K, (ii) ______ is converted into the active enzyme thrombin. Thrombin then converts the soluble plasma protein (iii) ______ into insoluble (iv) ______ threads that trap blood cells to form a stable clot.
why: **Name the substance released by injured tissue.** During coagulation, injured tissues and platelets release thromboplastin, which starts the clotting cascade, so (i) is thromboplastin.

**Identify the protein activated to thrombin.** In the presence of calcium ions and Vitamin K, thromboplastin brings about the conversion of the inactive plasma protein prothrombin into active thrombin, so (ii) is prothrombin.
**Identify the substrate of thrombin.** Thrombin acts as an enzyme on the soluble plasma protein fibrinogen, converting it into insoluble fibrin, so (iii) is fibrinogen and (iv) is fibrin.
**Interpret the final clot.** The insoluble fibrin threads form a mesh that traps blood cells, producing the stable clot that seals the break in the vessel.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q:
Complete the statements below about the first two stages of hemostasis.
In the first stage, called vascular spasm, the smooth muscle in the wall of the damaged vessel ______ in order to reduce blood loss. In the second stage, called the platelet plug, platelets adhere to the exposed ______, change shape and stick to each other to seal the break.
why: **Recall stage 1.** Vascular spasm is the contraction of the smooth muscle in the vessel wall, which narrows the vessel and reduces blood loss, so the first blank is 'contracts'.
**Recall stage 2.** In the platelet plug stage, platelets adhere to exposed collagen fibres of the damaged vessel, change shape and stick together, so the second blank is 'collagen'.
**Check the sequence.** The order is correct: vascular spasm first, platelet plug second, and coagulation third.

questions.q:
A patient in Asmara has a blocked bile duct and bruises and bleeds very easily. Complete the explanation below.
Vitamin K is needed by the ______ to produce the clotting factor ______. Vitamin K is ______-soluble, so it can only be absorbed in the small intestine when bile salts are present; when the bile duct is blocked, the production of this clotting factor falls and severe bleeding can occur.
why: **Locate the site of clotting-factor production.** Vitamin K is a necessary cofactor for the liver to produce the clotting factor prothrombin, so the first blank is 'liver' and the second is 'prothrombin'.
**Recall why bile is needed.** Vitamin K is fat-soluble and requires bile salts for absorption in the small intestine, so the third blank is 'fat'.

**Link the blockage to the symptom.** A blocked bile duct prevents Vitamin K absorption, the liver therefore makes too little prothrombin, and the clotting cascade fails, producing the easy bruising and bleeding described.

questions.q:
A blood bank in Asmara collects a $$200\text{ mL}$$ sample of whole blood from a donor. Plasma makes up $$55\%$$ of blood volume, and plasma is $$92\%$$ water.
(a) Calculate the volume of plasma in the sample.
(b) Calculate the volume of water contained in that plasma.
(c) Calculate the volume of the sample occupied by the cellular components (red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets).
questions.answer: (a) $$110\text{ mL}$$ of plasma; (b) $$101.2\text{ mL}$$ of water; (c) $$90\text{ mL}$$ of cellular components
why: **List the given data.** Total blood volume = $$200\text{ mL}$$; plasma = $$55\%$$ of blood volume; water = $$92\%$$ of plasma volume; cellular components = $$45\%$$ of blood volume (since $$100\% - 55\% = 45\%$$).
**Calculate the plasma volume.** Plasma volume = $$55\%$$ of $$200\text{ mL}$$ = $$0.55 \times 200 = 110\text{ mL}$$.
**Calculate the water in the plasma.** Water volume = $$92\%$$ of the plasma volume = $$0.92 \times 110 = 101.2\text{ mL}$$.
**Calculate the cellular volume.** Cellular volume = $$45\%$$ of $$200\text{ mL}$$ = $$0.45 \times 200 = 90\text{ mL}$$.
**Check the result.** The two parts must rebuild the whole sample: $$110\text{ mL} + 90\text{ mL} = 200\text{ mL}$$, which agrees with the given sample volume.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

**Calculate the cellular volume.** $$0.45 \times 250 = 112.5\text{ mL}$$; check $$137.5 + 112.5 = 250\text{ mL}$$.

**State the result clearly.** Just over half of the donated whole blood, $$227.7\text{ mL}$$, is water held in the plasma.

questions.q: During a blood-typing practical at a secondary school in Asmara, the red blood cells of a student are found to carry antigen B and antigen D (Rh), while the plasma contains anti-A antibodies. What is the student's blood group?
why: **Use the antigens to fix the ABO group.** The red cells carry antigen B and the plasma contains anti-A antibodies, which is exactly the pattern of blood group B (B antigen with anti-A antibody).
**Use antigen D to fix the Rh group.** The red cells also carry antigen D, and the presence of antigen D means the blood is Rh-positive; blood lacking antigen D is Rh-negative.

**Test the other options.** Options A and B require antigen A on the red cells, which is absent. Option D requires both A and B antigens and no antibodies in the plasma, but this student has anti-A antibodies.
**Conclude.** The only group matching antigen B, antigen D and anti-A antibodies is B Rh-positive.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: A patient in Keren is typed before surgery. The red blood cells carry no A antigen and no B antigen and lack antigen D, while the plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies. What is the patient's blood group?
why: **Interpret the absence of A and B antigens.** Red cells with neither A nor B antigen belong to group O, and such plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, exactly as described.
**Interpret the absence of antigen D.** Red cells that lack antigen D are Rh-negative, so the group is O Rh-negative.
**Eliminate the other options.** A Rh-negative carries A antigen; AB Rh-negative carries both A and B antigens and has no antibodies; O Rh-positive would carry antigen D, which is absent here.
**Conclude.** The patient is group O Rh-negative, the universal donor group.

questions.q: An Rh-negative mother has already given birth to one Rh-positive child. During a second pregnancy with an Rh-positive fetus, the fetus may develop erythroblastosis fetalis because:
questions.answer: A. The mother's anti-Rh antibodies cross the placenta and destroy the red blood cells of the fetus
why: **Explain how the mother becomes sensitised.** During the first pregnancy with an Rh-positive fetus, fetal red blood cells enter the Rh-negative mother's blood and stimulate her immune system to produce anti-Rh antibodies.
**Explain the effect in the second pregnancy.** In a later pregnancy with another Rh-positive fetus, these already formed anti-Rh antibodies cross the placenta and attack the fetal red blood cells.
**Name the outcome.** The destruction of fetal red blood cells produces the condition called erythroblastosis fetalis.

**Eliminate the distractors.** Option B reverses the direction of the antibodies, option C describes clumping of maternal cells rather than destruction of fetal cells, and option D wrongly replaces anti-Rh with anti-A antibodies.

questions.q:
A laboratory technician in Asmara measures the volume of water contained in the plasma of a patient's blood sample and records $$2.53\text{ L}$$. Plasma makes up $$55\%$$ of blood volume, and plasma is $$92\%$$ water.
(a) Calculate the volume of plasma in the sample.
(b) Calculate the patient's total blood volume.
(c) Calculate the volume occupied by the cellular components.
questions.answer: (a) $$2.75\text{ L}$$ of plasma; (b) $$5.0\text{ L}$$ of total blood; (c) $$2.25\text{ L}$$ of cellular components
why: **Set up the relationships.** Water is $$92\%$$ of plasma, so water $$= 0.92 \times$$ plasma. Plasma is $$55\%$$ of blood, so plasma $$= 0.55 \times$$ blood. The cellular components are the remaining $$45\%$$ of blood.
**Work backwards to the plasma volume.** Since $$0.92 \times \text{plasma} = 2.53\text{ L}$$, the plasma volume is $$\dfrac{2.53}{0.92} = 2.75\text{ L}$$.
**Work backwards to the total blood volume.** Since $$0.55 \times \text{blood} = 2.75\text{ L}$$, the total blood volume is $$\dfrac{2.75}{0.55} = 5.0\text{ L}$$.
**Calculate the cellular volume.** Cellular volume = total blood minus plasma = $$5.0\text{ L} - 2.75\text{ L} = 2.25\text{ L}$$, which also equals $$0.45 \times 5.0 = 2.25\text{ L}$$.
**Check the answer.** Plasma plus cells is $$2.75 + 2.25 = 5.0\text{ L}$$ of blood, and $$92\%$$ of the plasma is $$0.92 \times 2.75 = 2.53\text{ L}$$ of water, matching the measured value.

questions.q: The plasma water in a blood sample taken at a health centre in Asmara is measured as $$2.024\text{ L}$$. Plasma makes up $$55\%$$ of blood volume and plasma is $$92\%$$ water. Calculate the plasma volume, the total blood volume and the volume of the cellular components.
questions.answer: $$2.2\text{ L}$$ of plasma, $$4.0\text{ L}$$ of total blood and $$1.8\text{ L}$$ of cellular components
why: **Find the plasma volume.** $$\text{plasma} = \dfrac{2.024}{0.92} = 2.2\text{ L}$$.
**Find the total blood volume.** $$\text{blood} = \dfrac{2.2}{0.55} = 4.0\text{ L}$$.
**Find the cellular volume.** Cellular volume = $$4.0 - 2.2 = 1.8\text{ L}$$, which agrees with $$0.45 \times 4.0 = 1.8\text{ L}$$.
**Check.** $$2.2 + 1.8 = 4.0\text{ L}$$, and $$0.92 \times 2.2 = 2.024\text{ L}$$ of water, as given.

questions.q: The cellular components (red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets) of a patient's blood occupy $$3.6\text{ L}$$. Plasma makes up $$55\%$$ of blood volume and plasma is $$92\%$$ water. Calculate the patient's total blood volume, the plasma volume and the volume of water in that plasma.
questions.answer: $$8.0\text{ L}$$ of total blood, $$4.4\text{ L}$$ of plasma and $$4.048\text{ L}$$ (about $$4.05\text{ L}$$) of water
why: **Use the cellular percentage to find total blood.** Cellular components are $$45\%$$ of blood, so $$\text{blood} = \dfrac{3.6}{0.45} = 8.0\text{ L}$$.
**Find the plasma volume.** $$\text{plasma} = 0.55 \times 8.0 = 4.4\text{ L}$$, which also follows from $$8.0 - 3.6 = 4.4\text{ L}$$.
**Find the water in the plasma.** $$\text{water} = 0.92 \times 4.4 = 4.048\text{ L}$$, approximately $$4.05\text{ L}$$.
**Check.** $$4.4 + 3.6 = 8.0\text{ L}$$, so the plasma and cellular volumes rebuild the total blood volume correctly.
